Writing an adapter

Source: vignettes/adapters.Rmd
adapters.Rmd

If you have a class that represents a linear map, one method makes it work everywhere a linop works: in the algebra, in verify(), and in the solvers that arrive with the next phase. This vignette writes that method for a real operator, reads the certificate line by line, and then does the same job the other way, by registering a node type.

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

The example

A circulant matrix is determined by its first column, and it is applied by pointwise multiplication in the Fourier domain. An n by n circulant costs O(n log n) per apply and O(n) to store, so it is exactly the sort of operator that should never be written out.

conv <- function(w, X) {
  n <- length(w)
  Y <- X
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) {
    z <- fft(w * fft(X[, j]), inverse = TRUE) / n
    Y[, j] <- if (is.complex(X)) z else Re(z)
  }
  Y
}

w is the symbol, fft(col1). Two details in that function are the whole contract in miniature. The loop is over the columns of a block, because an apply always receives a matrix. The last line preserves the input type: a real block gives a real result, a complex block keeps its imaginary part.

One method

linop() is a generic dispatching on its first argument. An adapter defines linop.myclass() and returns a linop.

circulant <- function(col1) structure(list(col1 = col1), class = "circulant")

linop.circulant <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- length(x$col1)
  w <- fft(x$col1)
  linop(
    function(X) conv(w, X),
    adjoint = function(X) conv(Conj(w), X),
    dim = c(n, n),
    cost = 15 * n * log2(n)
  )
}

In a package, that method is registered with S3method(linop, circulant) in NAMESPACE, which roxygen2 writes from an @export tag on the method.

That is the whole adapter. The object now behaves like a matrix:

C <- linop(circulant(c(1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0)))
C
#> <linop> 6 x 6, double
#>   real
#> 
#> fun[6 x 6]
zapsmall(C %*% c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
#> [1] 1 2 3 0 0 0

and it composes:

N <- crossprod(C) + 0.1 * linop_eye(6)
N
#> <linop> 6 x 6, double
#>   hermitian, symmetric, positive_semidefinite, real
#> 
#> sum
#> |- product
#> |  |- transpose
#> |  |  `- fun[6 x 6]
#> |  `- fun[6 x 6]
#> `- scale by 0.1
#>    `- I[6]
cap(N, "hermitian")$value
#> [1] TRUE

The cost argument is worth passing. Without it a callback leaf assumes the dense flop count, 2 * nrow * ncol, which would make a fast operator look expensive to collapse() and to any future planner.

linop_cost(C)
#> [1] 232.6466
2 * 6 * 6      # what the default would have been
#> [1] 72

Reading the certificate 

verify(C)
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> adjoint consistency            pass         computation      identity              1
#> view identities                pass         computation      identity              1
#> real transpose equals adjoint  pass         computation      identity              1
#> linearity                      pass         computation      identity              1
#> block consistency              pass         computation      identity              1
#> shape and dtype                pass         computation      identity              1
#> complex linearity              pass         computation      identity              1
#> declared capabilities          not_checked  probe            heuristic             -
#> purity                         pass         computation      identity              1
#> gemm agreement                 pass         computation      identity              1
#> materialisation agreement      pass         computation      identity              1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: declared capabilities

Eleven checks, each reporting its own status, its source and the kind of guarantee it gives. This is one of four shapes the certificate takes, and the only one about the operator rather than about a computed result; vignette("certificates") covers the status and evidence columns, which are the same everywhere, and the other three shapes.

adjoint consistency tests <y, A x> = <A^H y, x> over random probe pairs. This is the check that earns its keep. A missing or misplaced conjugation is the most common bug in a hand-written operator, it produces an object that looks right under every casual test, and it makes every Krylov method built on it converge to the wrong answer. Here is the same adapter with Conj() dropped:

w <- fft(c(1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0))
Bad <- linop(function(X) conv(w, X),
             adjoint = function(X) conv(w, X),   # missing the conjugation
             dim = c(6, 6))
verify(Bad)
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> adjoint consistency            fail         computation      identity              1
#> view identities                pass         computation      identity              1
#> real transpose equals adjoint  pass         computation      identity              1
#> linearity                      pass         computation      identity              1
#> block consistency              pass         computation      identity              1
#> shape and dtype                pass         computation      identity              1
#> complex linearity              pass         computation      identity              1
#> declared capabilities          not_checked  probe            heuristic             -
#> purity                         pass         computation      identity              1
#> gemm agreement                 pass         computation      identity              1
#> materialisation agreement      pass         computation      identity              1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        fail   no deterministic bound on: declared capabilities
#> 
#> failures:
#>   adjoint consistency: max relative gap 3.652e+00

view identities checks that adjoint(t(A)), t(adjoint(A)) and adjoint(Conj(A)) act as they must. real transpose equals adjoint appears only for a real operator, and asserts both that the two act alike and that they remain distinct nodes.

linearity tests A(a x1 + b x2) = a A x1 + b A x2 with complex coefficients when the operator is complex. It is also what catches an adaptive solve that has been wrapped as an operator.

block consistency applies a block of several columns and compares each output column against applying that column alone. An operator that treats its input as a vector passes every scalar test and fails here.

shape and dtype applies real and complex blocks and checks the result shape, and that a complex input produces a complex output.

complex linearity tests A(x + iy) = A(x) + i A(y). This is the check that conv() was written to satisfy, in the line that keeps a complex block complex. An apply that discards the imaginary part of its input passes every other check in the suite, because the apply path promotes the real result it returned to complex before handing it back, which is enough to satisfy shape and dtype.

declared capabilities probes anything the operator claims about itself. Agreement is recorded as a probe beside the declaration; a contradiction fails the certificate. Nothing was declared above, so the line reads not_checked.

purity applies the same block twice and requires identical output and an unmodified input.

gemm agreement checks the two-tier apply. Authors implement tier one, apply(op, X, mode); solvers only ever call tier two, alpha * op(A) X + beta * Y, which is synthesised from tier one. This line confirms the synthesis matches.

materialisation agreement compares the dense form against applying the operator to the columns of an identity, when the operator is small enough to materialise at all.

The overall verdict is pass, qualified or fail. qualified means every check that ran passed and at least one did not run, so the certificate above is qualified only because nothing was declared to probe.

cert <- verify(C)
cert$overall
#> [1] "qualified"
cert$without_deterministic_bound
#> [1] "declared capabilities"

The certificate is a list, so a package can test against it directly:

stopifnot(verify(C)$overall %in% c("pass", "qualified"))

Declaring what you know

If the adapter knows a property, it should say so, and then verify() will probe it.

ws <- fft(c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0, -1))      # circularly symmetric kernel

Sym <- linop(function(X) conv(ws, X),
             adjoint = function(X) conv(Conj(ws), X),
             dim = c(6, 6),
             properties = c(symmetric = TRUE))
verify(Sym)$probes
#>   capability claimed gap    verdict
#> 1  hermitian    TRUE   0 consistent
#> 2  symmetric    TRUE   0 consistent

One declaration, two probe rows. A real symmetric operator is Hermitian by definition, so the closure applied at construction added the second claim and verify() probed both.

A declaration the operator does not honour is a failure rather than a warning:

wa <- fft(c(1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0))        # the asymmetric kernel from above

Liar <- linop(function(X) conv(wa, X),
              adjoint = function(X) conv(Conj(wa), X),
              dim = c(6, 6),
              properties = c(symmetric = TRUE))
verify(Liar)$probes
#>   capability claimed      gap      verdict
#> 1  hermitian    TRUE 9.141601 contradicted
#> 2  symmetric    TRUE 9.173422 contradicted
verify(Liar)$overall
#> [1] "fail"

The four modes

The four modes are the BLAS convention: N is A X, T is A^T X, C is A^H X, R is conj(A) X. A callback leaf supplies apply and adjoint, and the package derives T and R from them by conjugation, so an adapter author implements two functions and gets four modes.

That derivation is exact and it is not always the cheapest route. For a circulant operator the symbol of the transpose is the cyclic reversal of the symbol and the symbol of the adjoint is its conjugate, so each of the four is one multiply and the conjugation the derivation inserts is avoidable work. Where that matters the operator belongs in the package as a node type of its own, beside linop_eye() and linop_scaling(), rather than in a wrapper around a callback.

Complex kernels are the case worth testing, because they exercise all four modes independently:

wz <- c(1 + 1i, 2, 0, 0, 3 - 1i, 0)
Zc <- linop(function(X) conv(wz, X),
            adjoint = function(X) conv(Conj(wz), X),
            dim = c(6, 6))
verify(Zc)$overall
#> [1] "fail"

A materialisation trap worth knowing, found by running exactly this check on a node that built its own dense form: the first version used diag(1, n), a real identity, and conv() faithfully preserved the input type by discarding the imaginary part of a complex operator’s own columns. Every other line of the certificate passed and materialisation agreement failed with a gap of 1.0. If you materialise by applying to an identity, build that identity in the operator’s own dtype.

Preconditioners carry a contract

Two representations of a preconditioner are common, and mixing them is a recurring source of bugs: M approximating A and applied by solving M z = r, and P approximating A^-1 and applied as z = P r. Only one direction exists internally, apply_inverse, and the two constructors say which one you have.

D <- linop_scaling(c(4, 9, 16))

P1 <- as_preconditioner(D, solver = function(M, R) R / M$args$d)   # M ~ A
P2 <- as_preconditioner_inverse(linop_scaling(1 / c(4, 9, 16)))    # P ~ A^-1
P2
#> <preconditioner>
#>   side:              left
#>   fixed:             TRUE
#>   hermitian:         TRUE
#>   positive_definite: TRUE
#>   M^-H:              supplied

Both constructors read hermitian and positive_definite off the operator they were given, so a preconditioner built from a linop inherits what that operator knows.

Methods declare what they require, and a preconditioner that does not meet the requirement is refused by name. A flexible preconditioner, one whose map changes between applications, breaks the short recurrence that conjugate gradients is built on:

flexible <- preconditioner(function(R) R, fixed = FALSE)
flexible$fixed
#> [1] FALSE

Passing that to CG raises an error naming fixed and pointing at fgmres, which is the method designed to accept it. The requirement table covers cg, minres, gmres, fgmres, bicgstab, lsqr and lsmr, and it is enforced at the point the preconditioner is accepted rather than at the point the iteration misbehaves.

side is enforced on the same footing. FGMRES forms its update from the right-preconditioned basis, so it takes side = "right" and refuses the other two; the remaining methods admit more than one standard formulation and accept all three.

Solve objects are not operators

One boundary is worth knowing before the solvers land. An object is an operator if and only if its action on x is determined without reference to x. Conjugate gradients chooses its polynomial by minimising over the Krylov space of the right-hand side, so an approximate solve is not a linear operator, and it is not a linop.

Approximate solves are a separate class carrying a declared contract: whether the solve is exact, a fixed linear approximation, or variably inexact; whether it is fixed, input-dependent, or history-dependent; whether it is deterministic; whether an adjoint and an error bound are available. Consumers declare which contracts they accept, so an ordinary Arnoldi iteration cannot silently receive a history-dependent solve.

verify() dispatches on that class and tests the declared contract instead of assuming purity, and running the operator suite against one is an error that says why. The class is internal in this release; solve() is the public front door arriving with the next phase.

A checklist

Before shipping an adapter:

  1. verify() returns pass or qualified, on a real instance and, if the format supports it, a complex one.

  2. qualified is explained. Which check did not run, and why.

  3. Declared capabilities are honoured, and verify(x)$probes says consistent.

  4. cost is passed, so the operator is not mistaken for a dense matrix.

  5. Blocks of width greater than one behave, which block consistency covers.

  6. The apply does not modify its input, which purity covers.
